Hatach
HAY-tak
proper noun
Hebrew Hathak (H2047), a Persian name of uncertain meaning, sometimes read as verity or good; he is described as one of the king's chamberlains appointed to attend upon Esther.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Hatach was a chamberlain of Ahasuerus, appointed to wait upon Queen Esther, and he appears in exactly four verses at the hinge of the whole book. Mordecai had put on sackcloth and was crying in the street; Esther, shut in the palace, did not know why. Then called Esther for Hatach… and gave him a commandment to Mordecai, to know what it was, and why it was (Est 4:5). He went out to the street before the king's gate, received from Mordecai the account of Haman's decree and a copy of the writing, and carried it back; then Esther sent him out again, and again he went. He is the thread between the queen inside and the Jew outside at the moment when the survival of the covenant people hung on their being able to speak to one another. Then he vanishes from the record entirely. The book of Esther never once names God, and it is the most pointed book in the canon about His hidden working; Hatach is that argument in miniature. A Persian servant, doing an errand he did not understand, carried the message on which a nation's deliverance turned.

Origin & Era

A chamberlain of Ahasuerus appointed to attend Esther, who carried her messages to Mordecai and his to her at the crisis of the book.

expand to see more

HATACH, Hebrew Hathak, a Persian name of uncertain signification.

One of the king's chamberlains, whom Ahasuerus had appointed to attend upon Esther.

Esther sent him to Mordecai to learn the cause of his mourning.

He went forth to Mordecai unto the street of the city, before the king's gate.

He brought back to Esther the words of Mordecai and the copy of the decree.

Key Scripture

Est 4:5 — "Then called Esther for Hatach, one of the king's chamberlains, whom he had appointed to attend upon her, and gave him a commandment to Mordecai, to know what it was, and why it was."

Est 4:6 — "So Hatach went forth to Mordecai unto the street of the city, which was before the king's gate."

Est 4:9 — "And Hatach came and told Esther the words of Mordecai."

Est 4:10 — "Again Esther spake unto Hatach, and gave him commandment unto Mordecai;"

Modern Corruption

Providence is confused with coincidence; the book of Esther never names God and is the strongest proof in Scripture that He governs what He does not sign.

expand to see more

Because the name of God does not occur in Esther, the book is regularly read as a piece of secular court fiction, a nationalist tale that happened to be preserved. The reading mistakes reticence for absence. Every hinge in the story is a coincidence too convenient to be one: a king who cannot sleep and calls for the chronicles on precisely the right night; a gallows built for Mordecai that takes Haman; a Jewish girl already crowned queen before the decree that required her. Mordecai states the doctrine explicitly without using the divine name — who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this? (Est 4:14).

That is providence as the confessions define it: God upholding, directing, disposing and governing all creatures and all their actions, ordinarily through second causes and often invisibly. He does not need to be named to be at work, and the absence of miracles is not the absence of God. The principle to recover is that most of the Christian life is lived in Esther rather than in Exodus — no pillar of fire, no voice from heaven, only ordinary duties done in order, by people like Hatach who carry a message without knowing what hangs on it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Hathak (H2047), a Persian personal name; his office is saris (H5631), a chamberlain or eunuch of the court.

expand to see more

Hebrew Hathak (H2047) — the chamberlain who attended Esther; Esther 4:5, 4:6, 4:9, 4:10.

Hebrew saris (H5631) — a chamberlain, a eunuch, an officer of the royal household.

Hebrew Ester (H635) — Esther; her Hebrew name was Hadassah, myrtle (Est 2:7).

Hebrew et (H6256) — a time, a season; for such a time as this (Est 4:14).

Greek pronoia (G4307) — forethought, providence; the theological term for God's governing of all things.

Usage

"“Then called Esther for Hatach, one of the king's chamberlains”."

"“So Hatach went forth to Mordecai unto the street of the city”."

"“And Hatach came and told Esther the words of Mordecai”."
